claims.text: The relevant nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially form a single-phase solid solution.
High configurational entropy is the dominant factor governing structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K.
High configurational entropy suppresses atomic diffusion.
Configurational entropy raises the energy barriers for atomic rearrangement.
Suppressed atomic mobility hinders nucleation of secondary phases and ordered intermetallic compounds.
Sluggish diffusion prevents significant elemental migration and phase separation during high-temperature operation.
Suppression of diffusion maintains structural and chemical uniformity during catalytic or thermoelectric operation.
Equal- or near-equal-ratio high-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit minimal phase segregation across 473–1923 K.
The high-entropy nanoparticles will retain a single-phase solid-solution structure across the stated temperature range.
The high-entropy nanoparticles will maintain a stable chemical composition across the stated temperature range.
Nanoparticles engineered to have lower configurational entropy will undergo more phase separation or chemical reorganization under otherwise identical conditions.
Slight deviations from equal atomic ratios or selected doping can provide a lower-configurational-entropy comparison.
The proposed stabilization should hold primarily when oxidation and other external reactive influences are minimized.
In oxidative or extremely reactive environments, surface energy and chemical reactivity may override configurational-entropy stabilization.
The temperature thresholds and extent of phase stability may vary with nanoparticle composition and microstructure.
